analysis.one_liner: Wipes out a consumer bureau bulletin warning auto lenders about discriminatory loan pricing, and adds process requirements.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 332-96 in November 2015, with all 245 voting Republicans in favor, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill declares that a 2013 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau bulletin on indirect auto lending has no force or effect [S2] [S5]. That bulletin warned auto lenders they could be liable for discrimination when they let car dealers raise a borrower's interest rate above the rate the lender set — a practice studies showed tended to charge Black and Hispanic buyers more. The bill also requires the bureau to run a public comment period, disclose its underlying data, consult other agencies, and study costs before issuing any future guidance on indirect auto financing [S3] [S5]. It passed the House but never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Franchise auto dealers and the lenders that finance their sales. Keeping the dealer markup system intact lets dealers earn extra finance income on each loan, and nullifying the bulletin removes the warning that made their lending partners liable for discrimination caused by those markups [S2] [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies CFPB Bulletin 2013-02, the guidance that put lenders on notice they could be liable under fair-lending law for discriminatory dealer markups on car loans [S2] [S5].

Requires a public notice and comment period, public disclosure of all data relied on, redaction of exempt information, consultation with the Federal Reserve, FTC, and Justice Department, and a cost study before any future CFPB guidance primarily about indirect auto financing [S3] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers financing cars through dealers, especially Black and Hispanic borrowers, who studies found paid higher average markups; the bill removes the enforcement signal aimed at that practice [S2] [S5]. It also makes it harder for the consumer bureau to quickly warn lenders about fair-lending problems, since bulletins are meant to be a fast alternative to formal rulemaking.

drawbacks.text: By nullifying the bulletin, the bill eliminates the main warning tying lenders to liability for discriminatory dealer markups, the practice at the center of the bureau's fair-lending concern in auto finance [S2] [S5].

The added process requirements — comment periods, full data disclosure, and cost studies — would slow or deter the bureau from issuing informal guidance on auto lending, which is designed to be faster than formal rules [S3] [S5].

Supporters had a fair-process point: the bureau issued the bulletin without a comment period using confidential data, and dealers argued the transparency requirements and cost study were reasonable checks on that practice [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's transparency and consultation requirements could be defended on process grounds in isolation. But its concrete legal effect is to erase a fair-lending warning aimed at a pricing practice that cost borrowers money, so the balance favors dealers and lenders over consumers. The bill died, so those costs were never imposed.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 332-96 in November 2015, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: The bill nullifies CFPB Bulletin 2013-02 on indirect auto lending and adds notice-and-comment, disclosure, consultation, and cost-study requirements for future guidance on indirect auto financing [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5].
Introduced in April 2015 by Rep. Frank Guinta, it drew 166 cosponsors, 101 Republicans and 65 Democrats [S1] [S6] [S7].
The House Financial Services Committee ordered it reported 47-10 and reported it in November 2015 [S7].
The House passed it 332-96 on November 18, 2015; all 245 voting Republicans voted yes, and Democrats split 88 for and 96 against [S8].

The Senate received the bill on November 19, 2015 and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where no further action occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5] [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, especially minority car buyers, are better off because the bill died: the bulletin stayed in effect and the bureau kept its authority to address discriminatory dealer loan pricing, while dealers and lenders did not get the warning erased.

industries.note: Dealers earn finance income by marking up the interest rate a lender sets and keeping part of the increase. Nullifying the bulletin removes the warning that made lenders liable for discrimination caused by those markups, preserving the dealers' markup revenue at car buyers' expense.

industries.industry: Auto lenders and captive finance companies
industries.note: The bulletin put lenders on notice they could be liable under fair-lending law for discriminatory dealer markups on loans they financed. Nullifying it cuts that litigation and enforcement exposure, while the new process requirements make future fair-lending guidance harder to issue.

Not an industry, but the party on the other side of the pricing: the bill removes the enforcement signal against markup practices that studies found charged minority borrowers more, so borrowers would bear the cost if it became law.
